title: QUBO-Based Optimization of Social Indicator Configurations for Working-Age Population Growth
authors: Hayate Wada, Seiya Miyamoto, Tatsumasa Ogawa, Kazuki Uehara, Masaru Hitomi, Masayuki Ohzeki
abstract: The decline of the working-age population is a major challenge for regional sustainability, particularly in ageing societies such as Japan. We present a methodological demonstration of a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO)-based framework for exploring social-indicator configurations associated with working-age population growth. Using Japanese municipal data, we regressed the 2010-2020 working-age population growth rate on ten discretized social indicators. The resulting quadratic surrogate model showed reasonable predictive performance, with a test-set correlation coefficient of 0.84 and an average R-squared value of 0.76. Its coefficient matrix provides an interpretable representation of individual indicator-level contributions and pairwise associations. We converted the fitted model into a QUBO formulation with one-hot constraints and optimized it using quantum annealing, simulated annealing, and Gurobi. All three methods identified the same optimal feasible configuration, while the annealing-based samplers also generated feasible suboptimal configurations with different predicted growth rates. Municipality-level single-indicator analyses showed that changing one indicator can increase or decrease the predicted growth rate depending on the other indicators. The framework provides an interpretable and optimization-ready approach for connecting municipal social statistics, nonlinear interactions, and model-based scenario generation. It should be regarded as an exploratory tool for policy discussion rather than as a causal estimate of policy interventions.
summary: This paper applies a machine learning approach to model working-age population growth using local municipal social statistics. It formulates this relationship as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) problem and solves it using quantum annealing techniques. The framework provides an interpretable tool for exploring potential policy configurations, though its results are limited to model-based exploration rather than causal prediction.
main_problem: To develop an interpretable, optimization-ready framework connecting municipal social indicators to working-age population growth rates in aging societies.
main_result: The QUBO formulation successfully models the non-linear interactions between social indicators, and quantum/simulated annealing methods consistently find the optimal configuration predicted by exact solvers.
method: A quadratic surrogate model is fitted using regression on discretized social data, then converted into a QUBO Hamiltonian to be minimized via quantum or simulated annealing optimization.
model_or_system: The system models working-age population growth rate ($y$) as a function of ten discrete social indicators ($\vec{x}$), formulated as a quadratic objective function $G(\vec{x})$ subject to binary constraints.
key_observables: Test-set correlation coefficient (0.84) and average R-squared value (0.76); the optimal indicator configuration vector $\vec{x}_{opt}$.
important_parameters: The penalty coefficient ($\alpha=3$) used for enforcing one-hot constraints in the QUBO formulation.
main_assumptions: The framework is explicitly an exploratory tool, not a causal estimate of policy interventions; the model assumes quadratic relationships between indicator levels.
figures_summary: Figures show observed vs. fitted growth rates, heatmaps of the coefficient matrix $Q$ detailing pairwise interactions, and local sensitivity analyses showing predicted changes based on single-indicator flips.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the need for modeling population decline; it then details fitting a quadratic surrogate model to social data; this model is converted into a QUBO problem; finally, optimization using quantum/simulated annealing is performed and validated against exact solvers.
why_interesting: While applied to social science, the core methodology involves mapping complex combinatorial optimization problems onto QUBO Hamiltonians for solving with quantum annealers, which is relevant to general NISQ algorithm development.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Figure 1. Performance and coefficient structure of the quadratic surrogate model G(⃗x). (a) Observed working-age population growth rate y versus the fitted value G(⃗x) for all municipalities. The dashed line represents the ideal relation y = G(⃗x). The test-set correlation coefficient was 0.84, with an average mean squared error of 33.36 and an average coefficient of determination of R2 = 0.76 over 20 train–test splits. (b) Heatmap of the coefficient matrix of G(⃗x) for the 40 binary variables obtained from the one-hot encoding of ten social indicators. Diagonal elements correspond to individual binary-variable contributions, and off-diagonal elements correspond to pairwise interactions....

Figure 2. Sampling distributions obtained by simulated annealing and quantum annealing. The horizontal axis represents the surrogate value G(⃗x), corresponding to the predicted working-age population growth rate, and the vertical axis represents the number of samples. Only configurations satisfying the one-hot constraints are included. The vertical dashed line indicates the exact optimum obtained by Gurobi. The inset enlarges the low-count region to show feasible suboptimal configurations sampled by the annealing methods.

Figure 3. Predicted population growth rates, G(⃗x), obtained by virtually changing each municipal indicator by one discretized level for the three municipalities. The leftmost gray bar represents the prediction for the original feature vector⃗x, while the remaining bars represent the predictions obtained by changing only the corresponding indicator by one level, either decreasing (↓) or increasing (↑) it. The label ’Original’ denotes the original feature vector, and the other labels correspond to the municipal indicators listed in Table 1. Blue (red) bars indicate negative (positive) predicted population growth rates. The dashed line indicates the original predicted value.
